problem: Language-conditioned RL policies are built to map short instructions given at the start of an episode directly to actions. Their performance degrades when agents also receive other kinds of language that is only weakly correlated with optimal actions: world-state descriptions, dynamics or rules, corrections and game manuals.
motivation: Natural interaction with a household robot involves language beyond commands, such as 'I put the bowls away' or 'this button turns on the TV'. The mapping from such utterances to good actions depends on the task and is hard to learn from reward alone. The driving observation is that this language reliably helps predict the future: what the agent will observe, how the world will behave and what will be rewarded. Future prediction therefore gives a rich, self-supervised grounding signal.
key_idea: Treat language as another observation stream, one token per timestep. Train a DreamerV3-style multimodal world model to predict future latent representations of both text and images, then learn the policy by actor-critic in imagined rollouts. This separates grounding language (self-supervised prediction) from learning to act (RL).
insight: Grounding comes from next-representation prediction rather than from reward. On Messenger S1 the paper compares ways of adding language to DreamerV3: a language-conditioned policy, SentenceBERT sentence inputs, a T5 image adapter, and T5 cross-attention (frozen, finetuned or two-way). The simple scheme of one unaligned (image, token) pair per step, fed into the world model, beat all of them even with embeddings learned from scratch. Sentence-level inputs learned much more slowly. Among model-free baselines in HomeGrid, R2D2's score drops as hints are added while Dynalang's rises. Neither adding an auxiliary reconstruction loss to R2D2 nor scaling baselines to about 37M parameters closes the gap, which points to world modeling plus imagination-based policy learning as the source of the gain. A generative text model also enables text-only pretraining: TinyStories pretraining exceeds T5 embeddings on Messenger S2. It also enables KL-regularizing language actions toward the world model's next-token prediction, which makes RL with a 10k-token vocabulary tractable in LangRoom.
method: Multimodal alignment: at each timestep the agent receives one image frame and one language token (padded or zero when absent), with no semantic alignment assumed between them; it outputs a motor action and optionally a language token.

Multimodal RSSM world model (DreamerV3): a GRU sequence model predicts the next latent z_hat from (z_{t-1}, h_{t-1}, a_{t-1}). An encoder maps (image, token, h_t) to discrete categorical latents z_t via a strided CNN and a 5-layer MLP for language. A decoder reconstructs image, token, reward and continue flag. One-hot tokens use a cross-entropy loss; frozen T5-small token embeddings use MSE.

Losses: L_repr (image MSE, language cross-entropy, two-hot reward cross-entropy, binary cross-entropy for continue, KL regularizer with beta 0.1 and 1 free nat) plus L_pred = 0.5·max(1, KL[sg(z_t) || z_hat_t]). Predicting future representations forces extraction of information from language.

Policy learning by latent imagination: an unmodified DreamerV3 actor-critic (MLPs) is trained on 15-step imagined rollouts with lambda-returns, two-hot critic regression, percentile-normalized returns and an entropy bonus.

Text-only pretraining: image and action inputs are zeroed and the image, reward and continue loss weights set to 0, so the world model is trained on text corpora (Messenger manuals or TinyStories, about 500M tokens). The world model is then finetuned online with a freshly initialized actor and critic.

Language generation (LangRoom): the action space is extended with a token output, and the language action is KL-regularized toward the world model's predicted next token, sg(p(l_hat_{t+1})), to scale to a 10k vocabulary.

setting.backbone: DreamerV3-XL RSSM world model (GRU + CNN + MLPs) with actor-critic, trained from scratch by RL; frozen T5-small token embeddings as language input for Messenger and VLN-CE, one-hot tokens for HomeGrid and LangRoom
setting.training_data: Online RL experience only, with no expert demonstrations. For VLN-CE: 30M env steps sampling from the 10,819 R2R-CE training instructions over 61 scenes, 8 envs, about 16 A100 GPU-days. HomeGrid 50M steps; Messenger 1M/25M/50M steps for S1/S2/S3. Optional text-only pretraining on in-domain Messenger S2 manuals or TinyStories (2M GPT-4-generated stories, about 500M tokens).
setting.observation: VLN-CE: egocentric RGB + depth (64x64) plus a stream of T5-embedded instruction tokens, one per step. HomeGrid/LangRoom: partial-view pixels plus a token stream. Messenger: symbolic 16x16 entity grid plus manual tokens.
setting.action_space: VLN-CE: low-level FORWARD 0.25 m / TURN LEFT/RIGHT 15° / STOP. Other environments: discrete grid moves and interactions; LangRoom adds a language-token action.
setting.simulator: Habitat (VLN-CE on Matterport3D); also custom HomeGrid, Messenger and LangRoom gridworlds
setting.privileged: none at test time. During VLN-CE training the agent uses a dense shaped reward based on the change in distance to the goal, a +1000 success reward and a −10 penalty for a wrong stop.

numbers_note: All quantitative results appear only in figures (bar charts and training curves); the paper has no numeric results tables. The VLN-CE result (Fig. 'VLN-CE results') is success rate plotted over RL training, averaged across 3 seeds for Dynalang and 2 for R2D2, apparently measured on the training instructions rather than on val-unseen. It is described only qualitatively ('succeeds at significantly more instructions compared to the model-free R2D2 baseline'), with the admission that it is 'not yet competitive with state-of-the-art VLN methods'. HomeGrid, Messenger, LangRoom and text-pretraining results are likewise figure-only.
results: On HomeGrid (50M steps), Dynalang scores higher with each hint type (future observations, dynamics, corrections) than with task-only language. It outperforms IMPALA and R2D2 even with task-only language; IMPALA barely learns and R2D2 degrades as hints are added. On Messenger, Dynalang beats EMMA, IMPALA and R2D2 and is the only method to reach non-trivial performance on Stage 3. On VLN-CE it learns instruction following from scratch with RL and succeeds on significantly more instructions than R2D2, though it is far from SOTA VLN-CE methods. TinyStories text-only pretraining surpasses T5 embeddings on Messenger S2. No numeric values are printed for any of these results.
limitations: VLN-CE performance is not competitive with state-of-the-art methods such as ETPNav or waypoint-based agents. The reported curve reflects training-time success, not a standard val-unseen evaluation with SR/SPL.

Language is mostly scripted or template-generated (HomeGrid hints, Messenger templates, LangRoom questions) and environments are small gridworlds. Scaling to open-ended natural human language is left to future work.
Training is expensive and sample-hungry: tens of millions of environment steps, and 16 GPU-days for VLN-CE and 24 for Messenger S3.
